title: UA spacecraft eyes asteroid Apophis in rare 2029 flyby

content:
TUCSON, Ariz. (KVOA) - A NASA spacecraft is on course to witness a rare celestial event when the asteroid Apophis passes within about 20,000 miles of Earth's surface on April 13, 2029, closer than satellites carrying TV broadcasts and satellite images.

OSIRIS-APEX, which previously flew as OSIRIS-REx and brought a sample of the asteroid Bennu back to Earth in September 2023, is expected to reach Apophis in late spring of 2029, according to the University of Arizona. An asteroid this size comes so close to Earth only once about every 7,500 years.

"I think that's just going to be a really powerful sequence of images to help people understand how vulnerable we are," DellaGiustina said.

Dani Mendoza DellaGiustina, associate professor at the Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and the principal investigator of OSIRIS-APEX, said the spacecraft will capture images of the asteroid sliding past the side of Earth where night has fallen, over Europe and northern Africa. Millions of people will be able to watch it with their own eyes.

The team is currently writing commands the spacecraft will follow when it swings past Earth next March. That flyby is one of several gravity assists built into the mission's route, in which the spacecraft passes close to Earth and borrows some of our planet's energy to reshape its own path around the sun.

The last flyby in September 2025 gave the team a chance to point the instruments to Earth. DellaGiustina said the team has made a significant discovery in the data collected during the 2025 flyby.

"Studying Earth as a habitable world from the perspective of a distant spacecraft that is seeing our own planet as it though it's an astronomical object is a really rare opportunity," DellaGiustina said.

Getting to Apophis involved making innovations with the spacecraft itself. The route requires an orbit that carries the spacecraft much closer to the sun than it was designed to survive.

To get through the passes, engineers tilt the spacecraft's wing-like solar panels so that they cast shade over its heat-sensitive parts. DellaGiustina said the approach has worked so far, though three more close passes remain.

Once the spacecraft reaches Apophis in late spring 2029, the big question is what Earth's gravity will do to the asteroid. As Earth's gravity pulls on Apophis during the close approach, the asteroid will shake hard enough that material on its surface could be thrown upward.

"OSIRIS-APEX will be in a unique geometry to observe that shaking, which is very cool," DellaGiustina said.

The mission has a few students on the team now. OSIRIS-REx trained more than 150, many of whom went on to work for NASA and its industry partners.

"It's a really important and personal part of our story – the number of students that we've trained," DellaGiustina said. "We'll continue to do that as we start ramping up our staffing the closer we get to arriving at Apophis."
